subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The GM EV1 Experiment
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The GM EV1 Experiment.

hook.text: In 1996, General Motors released the EV1—the first modern electric car from a major automaker.

buildup.text: It was sleek, fast, and fully electric. Drivers loved it. Celebrities leased them in California.

discovery.text: GM only offered leases, never sales. About 1,100 were produced over three years.

twist.text: In 2003, GM canceled the program and crushed nearly every EV1. Owners begged to buy them.

climax.text: The documentary 'Who Killed the Electric Car?' blamed oil companies, dealers, and GM itself.

punchline.text: GM built the future—then destroyed it.

quiz.question: What happened to most GM EV1 cars?

details.summary: General Motors' EV1, produced from 1996 to 1999, was the first mass-produced electric car from a major automaker, but GM controversially recalled and crushed nearly all of them, becoming a symbol of corporate resistance to EVs.
details.whyItMatters: The EV1's destruction became a rallying cry for EV advocates and inspired the documentary Who Killed the Electric Car. It demonstrated that viable EVs could be built but also that industry politics could kill them.
takeaways: The EV1 was leased to customers, never sold outright
GM recalled and crushed nearly all 1,100 vehicles produced
The controversy inspired the 2006 documentary about EV suppression

faq.question: Why did GM destroy the EV1?
faq.answer: GM cited low demand, expensive battery replacements, and the end of California's zero-emission mandate. Critics believe GM bowed to oil industry pressure and feared the EV1 would cannibalize its profitable gasoline car business.

faq.question: Did the EV1 influence Tesla's creation?
faq.answer: Indirectly, yes. The EV1 proved consumer appetite for electric cars existed. Its destruction motivated activists and entrepreneurs, including some who later supported or joined Tesla, to prove that EVs deserved a second chance.
